title: Elements • Book III • Proposition 36
subtitle: Tangent-Secant Theorem
Visual description: Given circle ABC, external point D, secant DCA cutting the circle at C and A, and tangent DB touching at B.
narration: Elements, Book three, Proposition thirty-six. From a point outside a circle, if a secant line cuts the circle and a tangent line touches it, the rectangle contained by the whole secant and its external segment equals the square on the tangent. Let point D be taken outside circle A B C, let secant D C A cut the circle at C and A, and let D B touch the circle at B. We claim that the rectangle A D by C D equals the square on tangent D B.

subslides.enunciation: If a point be taken outside a circle and from it there fall on the circle two straight lines, and if one of them cut the circle and the other touch it, the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference will be equal to the square on the tangent.

title: Radius to the Point of Contact
subtitle: Construction
Visual description: Join radius FB from center F to point of contact B; by III.18, angle FBD is a right angle.
narration: When secant D C A passes through the center F, join radius F B from the center to the point of contact B. By Book three Proposition eighteen, the radius F B is perpendicular to the tangent D B, making angle F B D a right angle.

title: Extended Bisected Segment & Pythagorean Theorem
subtitle: Demonstration
Visual description: By II.6, rect(AD, CD) + sq(FC) = sq(FD); since FC = FB, rect(AD, CD) + sq(FB) = sq(FD) = sq(FB) + sq(DB) by I.47, so rect(AD, CD) = sq(DB).
narration: Since diameter A C is bisected at the center F and extended in a straight line by C D, Book two Proposition six states that the rectangle A D by C D plus the square on F C equals the square on F D. Because radii F C and F B are equal, we can substitute the square on F B, so the rectangle A D by C D plus the square on F B equals the square on F D. By the Pythagorean theorem on right triangle F B D, the square on F B plus the square on D B also equals the square on hypotenuse F D. Subtracting the common square on F B leaves the rectangle A D by C D equal to the square on tangent D B, as was required to prove.

title: Exterior Power of a Point & Dependency Graph
subtitle: Commentary & Genealogy
Visual description: Commentary on Case 2 (non-central secant) and the two-secants corollary, followed by the G.144 genealogy card.
narration: When the secant does not pass through the center, Euclid drops a perpendicular from the center to bisect chord A C and applies the Pythagorean theorem twice to reach the exact same identity. Together with Proposition thirty-five, this completes the exterior Power of a Point theorem: for any secant from D, the product A D by C D equals the square on tangent D B—and therefore any two secants from the same external point contain equal rectangles. In the GEOMETOR dependency graph, Proposition thirty-six unites sixty ancestor nodes across Books one, two, and three, and directly powers both its converse in Proposition thirty-seven and the golden-triangle construction for the regular pentagon in Book four Proposition ten.

subslides.commentary_body: In Euclid's second case, when secant / D C A / does not pass through the center, a perpendicular from the center bisects chord / A C / (III.3), and adding the square on that perpendicular via II.6 and I.47 yields the same relation. As Heath notes, two immediate corollaries follow: any two secants from D contain equal rectangles, and the two tangents from D are equal.
